evidence.note: The agent decided to 'generate a single halyard.py' implementing the entire ~dozen-subsystem service in one monolithic push — no ordered milestone hierarchy, no dependency-aware build sequencing (SigV4/storage front-loaded before multipart/versioning). Decomposition into ordered sub-goals is essentially absent at the construction stage.

During verification the agent does enumerate major subsystems and address them in a sensible sequence (core CRUD/presign/copy first, then multipart, versioning, ranges, policy, admin/audit), showing subsystem awareness and rough per-area done-checks (smoke test passes), but this is organized testing rather than an upfront milestone plan with acceptance criteria.

Finalization added one more targeted patch (conditional If-Match PUT) and reset state — the 'done' notion is 'all my smoke tests pass', a rough end-check rather than explicit per-milestone acceptance criteria defined and sequenced in advance.

Per-step 'Plan:' lines are tactical next-actions (get server running, install deps, fix imports), not a living dependency-aware milestone plan; foundations were reached implicitly (app must run to health-check) rather than through deliberate risk-first sequencing.

reasoning: The agent built the whole service as one monolithic file with no explicit milestone hierarchy, ordering rationale, or per-milestone acceptance checks defined upfront, which keeps it below the level-5/8 anchors that require dependency-aware sequencing and front-loaded foundational risk. However, it is above the flat-vague-to-do of anchor 3: during iteration it enumerated the major subsystems and worked through them in a sensible order with rough done-checks via smoke tests. That mix of monolithic construction plus subsystem-aware, roughly-verified iteration places it at a 4, just short of the clean 'enumerate and tackle in sensible order' of anchor 5.
